question:
Select the word that is similar in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below
Craven
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cowardly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Craven" means contemptibly lacking in courage; cowardly — showing shameful fear when facing danger, pain, or difficulty. (कायर, डरपोक)
◦ Example: He gave a craven excuse to avoid confronting the bully.

• Both "Craven" and "Cowardly" describe a marked lack of bravery and an unwillingness to face danger or hardship, making them close synonyms.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Bold" (साहसी): means confident, daring and courageous — this is an antonym of craven, not a synonym.

• Option 2: "Unabashed" (निडर, बेशर्म): means not embarrassed or ashamed; showing no sign of guilt or shyness — unrelated to physical courage.

• Option 4: "Gallant" (वीर, बहादुर): means brave, heroic and chivalrous — again an antonym, not a synonym, of craven.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Craven": pusillanimous, timorous, faint-hearted, spineless, dastardly.

• Do not confuse "Craven" (cowardly) with the verb "Crave" (to long for something intensely) — the two words are unrelated in meaning despite the similar spelling.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Coarse
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Buttery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Coarse" means rough or harsh in texture; lacking in fineness or smoothness (and, of manners or speech, crude or vulgar). (खुरदरा, अपरिष्कृत)
◦ Example: The coarse fabric felt scratchy against her skin.

• "Buttery" means smooth, soft and rich, like butter — the exact opposite quality of texture to "coarse", which makes it the best antonym among the options given.
◦ Example: The sauce had a smooth, buttery texture.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Devoted" (समर्पित): means very loving, loyal or dedicated to a person or cause — it relates to loyalty, not texture, so it is not an antonym of coarse.

• Option 3: "Unrefined" (अपरिष्कृत): actually means rough, crude and not processed to remove impurities — this is a synonym, not an antonym, of coarse, so it is incorrect.

• Option 4: "Gruntled" (संतुष्ट): an informal word meaning satisfied or pleased (a back-formation from "disgruntled") — it concerns mood, not texture, so it is unrelated here.

NOTE

• Other antonyms of "Coarse": fine, smooth, delicate, refined, polished.

• Other synonyms of "Coarse": rough, crude, unpolished, vulgar, harsh.

question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Beneficiel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Beneficial", not "Beneficiel" — meaning favourable or advantageous; producing good results.
◦ Example: Regular exercise is beneficial for overall health.

• Spelling key: BENE + FIC + IAL. The word ends in "-cial", not "-ciel"; many candidates wrongly swap the "ia" for "ie" by analogy with French-looking endings.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Benign" is correctly spelt — it means gentle, kindly, or (of a tumour) not harmful.

• Option 2: "Besiege" is correctly spelt — it means to surround with armed forces, or to overwhelm with requests.

• Option 4: "Bifurcate" is correctly spelt — it means to divide into two branches or parts.

NOTE

• Other words ending in "-cial" that are commonly misspelt in SSC exams: official, financial, artificial, commercial, judicial, superficial.

• Related words: benefit, beneficiary, beneficence — all keep the "bene-" root meaning "good/well".

question:
Some parts of a sentence have been jumbled up, and labelled P, Q, R and S. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
Many retailers have invested
P. time and money into understanding its
Q. make them healthier so they can continue to be marketed
R. promotions work, and changing product ingredients to
S. complexity, refitting shops, trialling which healthier
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. PSRQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence opens with the independent clause "Many retailers have invested", which needs an object to complete its meaning — this is supplied by P: "time and money into understanding its", giving "invested time and money into understanding its [something]".

• The word "its" at the end of P needs a noun to refer to, which is supplied by S: "complexity, refitting shops, trialling which healthier" — continuing the list of actions retailers have invested in (understanding its complexity, refitting shops, trialling which healthier promotions work).

• S ends with "trialling which healthier", which is completed by R: "promotions work, and changing product ingredients to" — giving "trialling which healthier promotions work, and changing product ingredients to [do something]".

• Finally, Q: "make them healthier so they can continue to be marketed" completes the purpose clause begun by "to" at the end of R, closing the sentence with a clear final goal.

• Reading the parts together in the order P-S-R-Q gives a single, logically connected sentence: "Many retailers have invested time and money into understanding its complexity, refitting shops, trialling which healthier promotions work, and changing product ingredients to make them healthier so they can continue to be marketed."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: SRPQ is incorrect because it places S directly after the opening line, but S begins with "complexity", which has no antecedent noun until "its" (from P) has appeared — S cannot logically come before P.

• Option 3: PQRS is incorrect because it jumps straight from P to Q ("make them healthier..."), producing the purpose clause before the actions (refitting shops, trialling promotions) that it is meant to follow — this breaks the logical cause-and-effect order.

• Option 4: QRPS is incorrect because it starts the sentence with the purpose clause Q ("make them healthier so they can continue to be marketed"), which cannot logically follow directly after "Many retailers have invested" without first stating what was invested in.

NOTE

• In para-jumble/rearrangement questions, first identify the part that logically follows the fixed opening sentence (here, an object is needed for "invested"), then trace pronoun references ("its") and connecting words ("and", "to") to link the remaining parts in sequence.

• Always read the final assembled sentence once fully to confirm it makes complete grammatical and logical sense before marking the answer.

question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Camor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Clamor" (or "Clamour" in British spelling), not "Camor" — meaning a loud and confused noise, or a vehement public expression of protest or demand.
◦ Example: There was a clamour among the crowd for the referee's decision to be reversed.

• Spelling key: the word begins with "Cla-", not "Ca-" — the letter "l" has been dropped from the given option, which is the error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Circumspect" is correctly spelt — it means careful to consider all circumstances and possible consequences before acting.

• Option 3: "Cloying" is correctly spelt — it means distasteful through being excessive or overly sweet/sentimental.

• Option 4: "Coffer" is correctly spelt — it means a strongbox or chest for holding valuables, or (in plural) financial reserves.

NOTE

• Commonly confused/misspelt words with silent or dropped letters in SSC exams: acquaint, colleague, conscience, government, foreign, rhythm.

• Remember the British spelling "clamour" and American spelling "clamor" are both acceptable; only the missing "l" makes "Camor" wrong.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Just one ______ of paper can lead to a whole lot of fun.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. sheet.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "sheet" is the correct collective/measure word used for a single flat piece of paper — the phrase "a sheet of paper" is a fixed collocation in English.
◦ Example: She wrote her address on a blank sheet of paper.

• A collocation is a natural combination of words that native speakers use habitually; "sheet of paper" is one of the most common paper-related collocations tested in SSC exams.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "bunch" is used for a cluster of similar items tied or grouped together, such as "a bunch of flowers/keys/bananas" — not for a single sheet of paper.

• Option 3: "bulk" refers to a large mass or quantity of something, such as "goods sold in bulk" — it does not collocate with a single piece of paper.

• Option 4: "group" refers to a number of people or things considered together — it is too general and does not form a natural collocation with "paper".

NOTE

• Other common collocations with measure words: a loaf of bread, a flock of birds, a herd of cattle, a pack of cards, a ream of paper (500 sheets).

• "Sheet" can also be used for other flat items: a sheet of glass, a sheet of metal, a bedsheet.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The cat ate all the pastries.
option_1: All the pastries is eaten by the cat.
option_2: All the pastries were eaten by the cat.
option_3: All the pastries had been eaten by the cat.
option_4: All the pastries are eaten by the cat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. All the pastries were eaten by the cat.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The cat ate all the pastries." is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "all the pastries" becomes the subject of the passive sentence; since "pastries" is plural, the auxiliary used is "were"; the verb "ate" becomes its past participle "eaten"; and "the cat" becomes the agent introduced by "by".
◦ Passive: All the pastries were eaten by the cat.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "is eaten" is present tense and also does not agree in number with the plural subject "pastries" (it should be "are", not "is", even in the present tense).

• Option 3 is incorrect because "had been eaten" is the passive form of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Simple Past Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "are eaten" is the passive form of the Simple Present Tense, not the Simple Past Tense.

NOTE

• Always match the tense of the passive auxiliary to the tense of the active sentence; only the subject-object positions and the verb form change, the tense must remain identical.

• Subject-verb agreement applies to the passive auxiliary as well: singular subject → is/was; plural subject → are/were.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
A guru is someone who does not charge you a fee because someone who is tied in greed couldn't release you.
option_1: charge you a fee because someone
option_2: who is tied in greed couldn't release you.
option_3: A guru is someone who does not
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. who is tied in greed couldn't release you.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence makes a general, timeless statement about what a guru is, using the Simple Present Tense throughout: "is someone", "does not charge", "is tied".

• Rule — Tense Consistency: when a sentence expresses a general truth or definition in the present tense, every verb in the sentence (including modals) must remain in the present tense unless there is a clear reason to shift.

• The segment "who is tied in greed couldn't release you" wrongly uses the past modal "couldn't" (could not), which breaks the tense consistency of the sentence. It should be "can't release you" (present tense) to match "is someone" and "does not charge".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "charge you a fee because someone" is grammatically correct as part of the present-tense statement and contains no error.

• Option 3: "A guru is someone who does not" is grammatically correct — the subject-verb agreement ("guru...is") and the auxiliary "does not" are both properly used.

• Option 4: "No error" is incorrect because an error does exist, as explained above, in the segment given in Option 2.

NOTE

• A frequent SSC error-spotting trap is a sudden, unjustified shift between present and past tense (or between modals like can/could, will/would) within the same sentence.

• Other commonly tested modal pairs: can/could, shall/should, will/would, may/might — each pair carries a present vs. past (or more tentative) sense and must match the surrounding tense.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
Buddy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Associate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Buddy" means a close friend or companion, someone with whom one shares a friendly, informal relationship. (मित्र, साथी)
◦ Example: He and his buddy have been inseparable since childhood.

• "Associate" means a person who is joined with another in some activity, business, or friendly relationship — among the given options, it is the closest in meaning to "buddy" as a companion/fellow person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Stylist" (केश-सज्जाकार/शैलीकार): a person who designs or advises on hairstyles, clothing, or overall appearance — unrelated to friendship.

• Option 2: "Foe" (शत्रु): means an enemy or opponent — this is an antonym, not a synonym, of "buddy".

• Option 4: "Enemy" (दुश्मन): means a person who is hostile to another — again an antonym, not a synonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Buddy": companion, pal, mate, comrade, chum.

• Antonym pairs frequently tested alongside this word: friend ↔ foe, ally ↔ enemy, companion ↔ stranger.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Jejune
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Drab.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Jejune" means dull, uninteresting, and lacking in substance or nourishment; it can also mean naive or simplistic (when used of ideas). (नीरस, फीका)
◦ Example: The critics dismissed the film's plot as jejune and uninspired.

• "Drab" means dull, dreary, and lacking in brightness or interest — this matches the "dull/uninteresting" sense of "jejune" among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Poignant" (मार्मिक): means evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret; deeply moving — this is essentially opposite in feel to the dullness implied by "jejune".

• Option 3: "Unchildlike": means not resembling or behaving like a child — unrelated to the meaning of "jejune".

• Option 4: "Cosmopolitan" (विश्वजनीन): means familiar with and at ease in many different countries and cultures — unrelated in meaning to "jejune".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Jejune": insipid, banal, vapid, dry, uninspired.

• Do not confuse "jejune" with "juvenile" — though they sound similar, "juvenile" specifically means relating to young people or being childish, while "jejune" centres on dullness or naivety.

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Pick the option that gives their correct order.
P. The average adult gets two to four colds a year, while the average child may get six to eight.
Q. It is the most frequent infectious disease in humans.
R. They occur more commonly during the winter.
S. The common cold, also known simply as the cold, is a viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that primarily affects the nose.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. SQPR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A logically ordered passage should begin with a sentence that introduces and defines the topic. S: "The common cold, also known simply as the cold, is a viral infectious disease of the upper respiratory tract that primarily affects the nose." does exactly this, so it must come first.

• Having defined the cold, the next logical step is to state a general fact about its prevalence, which is given by Q: "It is the most frequent infectious disease in humans."

• After establishing that it is the most frequent infectious disease, the passage naturally moves to supporting statistics, given by P: "The average adult gets two to four colds a year, while the average child may get six to eight."

• Finally, R: "They occur more commonly during the winter." adds a further specific detail (seasonal pattern) and fittingly closes the passage.

• Reading S-Q-P-R together produces a coherent, logically flowing paragraph: definition → general fact → supporting statistic → seasonal detail.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: QSRP is incorrect because it opens with the pronoun "It" in Q, which has no antecedent noun until S (which names "the common cold") appears — Q cannot logically precede S.

• Option 3: QPSR is incorrect for the same reason: it begins with "It", leaving the pronoun without a clear referent, and additionally separates the definition (S) from the fact it explains (Q).

• Option 4: PQRS is incorrect because it opens with a specific statistic (P) about colds before the subject "the common cold" has even been introduced or defined (S), leaving the reader without context.

NOTE

• In jumbled-paragraph questions, always locate the sentence that introduces the topic by full name/definition (rather than a pronoun) — that sentence must open the passage.

• Track pronouns like "it", "they", "this" carefully; they must always refer back to a noun already mentioned in an earlier sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
New kid on the block
option_2: Savings set aside for future use.
option_3: Don't hurt anyone that helps you.
option_4: Someone new to the group or area.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Someone new to the group or area.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "New kid on the block" means a person who has recently joined a group, organisation, neighbourhood, or field, and is not yet familiar to the others there. (नया सदस्य/नवागंतुक)
◦ Example: As the new kid on the block, she took a few weeks to learn everyone's names in the office.

• The phrase originated from the literal image of a new child moving into a neighbourhood ("block") who has not yet been accepted or gotten to know the other children living there.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Nonsense or meaningless speech" describes idioms like "mumbo jumbo" or "gibberish", not "new kid on the block".

• Option 2: "Savings set aside for future use" describes an idiom like "a nest egg", not "new kid on the block".

• Option 3: "Don't hurt anyone that helps you" resembles the sense of an idiom like "don't bite the hand that feeds you", not "new kid on the block".

NOTE

• Other idioms about newcomers/inexperience: "Wet behind the ears" (inexperienced), "Fresh off the boat" (newly arrived, unfamiliar with local customs), "Learn the ropes" (to learn how to do a job or task).

• Idioms about belonging to a place: "To feel at home", "To find one's feet".

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
Cast someone adrift
option_1: To leave someone without any support or purpose
option_4: To blame someone for one's mistakes
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To leave someone without any support or purpose.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Cast someone adrift" means to abandon or leave someone without help, guidance, direction, or means of support. (असहाय छोड़ देना)
◦ Example: When the company shut down without notice, hundreds of workers were cast adrift with no income.

• The phrase comes from a nautical image: a boat that is "set adrift" is cut loose from its moorings and left to float without control or direction — applied figuratively to a person left without support.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "To change plan suddenly" describes an idiom like "to do a U-turn" or "to change tack", not "cast adrift".

• Option 3: "Call someone repeatedly" does not match this idiom at all; it is unrelated to the nautical sense of "adrift".

• Option 4: "To blame someone for one's mistakes" describes an idiom like "to pass the buck" or "to scapegoat someone", not "cast adrift".

NOTE

• Other nautical idioms common in SSC exams: "To rock the boat" (to disturb a stable situation), "To be in the same boat" (to be in the same difficult situation as others), "To batten down the hatches" (to prepare for trouble).

• Related idiom: "To leave someone in the lurch" — to abandon someone in a difficult situation without help.

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
It was past the mid-hour of the night, and was quite ______ and dark.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. moonless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "moonless" means without any moon or moonlight visible in the sky — it fits naturally with "and dark" to describe the state of the night sky at that hour.
◦ Example: On a moonless night, the stars appeared unusually bright.

• The blank requires an adjective describing the condition of the night sky, paired logically with "dark"; "moonless" (no moon) directly complements "dark" (no light), giving a coherent description of a pitch-black night.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "glimmer" is a noun/verb meaning a faint or unsteady light — it is not an adjective and cannot grammatically fill the blank before "and dark".

• Option 3: "flasher" refers to a device or person that flashes (or, informally, an indecent exposer) — it does not fit the description of a night sky at all.

• Option 4: "riding" is a present participle relating to travel on a horse/vehicle — it has no logical connection to describing a dark night.

NOTE

• Compound adjectives formed with "-less" are common in SSC vocabulary questions: moonless, starless, cloudless, sleepless, endless.

• Always check that the chosen word matches the part of speech required by the sentence — here, only an adjective can grammatically follow "quite" and precede "and dark".

question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, then select the option "No error".
I felt that / I was be groomed / for success in the world.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. I was be groomed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "I was be groomed" is grammatically incorrect because it places two verb forms — "was" and "be" — consecutively, which is not permissible in standard English.

• Rule: the passive voice in the past tense is formed as Subject + was/were + V3 (past participle). The correct form here should be either "I was groomed" (simple past passive) or "I was being groomed" (past continuous passive), but never "was be groomed".

• Correcting the segment: "I felt that I was groomed for success in the world."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because a clear grammatical error exists in the segment identified in Option 2.

• Option 3: "I felt that" is grammatically correct — "felt" is the correct simple past form of "feel", and "that" correctly introduces the noun clause that follows.

• Option 4: "for success in the world." is grammatically correct — the prepositional phrase is properly formed and correctly completes the sentence.

NOTE

• A double/auxiliary verb clash (e.g., "was be", "is be", "has be") is a frequently tested SSC error — remember that "be" only follows a modal (can be, will be, should be, must be), never directly after "was/were/is/am/are".

• Passive voice forms to remember: Simple Past — was/were + V3; Past Continuous — was/were + being + V3; Past Perfect — had been + V3.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A lover of good food
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Gourmand.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Gourmand" is a person who takes great pleasure in eating and drinking, especially one who enjoys good food in large quantities. (खाने-पीने का शौकीन)
◦ Example: As a true gourmand, he never turns down an invitation to a fine dinner.

• The word is French in origin and traditionally implies a hearty enjoyment of food, sometimes bordering on excess, as distinguished from a "gourmet" (a connoisseur of fine food and refined taste).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Esoteric" (गूढ़): means intended for or understood by only a small, specialised group; obscure or abstruse — unrelated to food.

• Option 2: "Chauvinist" (कट्टर राष्ट्रवादी/पक्षपाती): means a person who is excessively or unreasonably devoted to their own group, cause, or gender — unrelated to food.

• Option 4: "Ergophile": a person who loves work — unrelated to food; the opposite of "ergophobe" (one who fears/dislikes work).

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions about food: Gourmet — a connoisseur of good food and wine; Glutton — a person who eats and drinks excessively; Epicure — a person devoted to sensual, especially culinary, pleasures; Vegan/Vegetarian — one who abstains from animal products/meat.

• Commonly confused pair: Gourmand (hearty love of food, often in quantity) vs. Gourmet (refined, expert taste in food).

question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.
I said, 'I'm not very happy at work.'
option_1: I told her that I was not very happy at work.
option_2: I told her I would not be very happy at work.
option_3: I told her that I had not been very happy at work.
option_4: I told her I am not very happy at work.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I told her that I was not very happy at work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct speech "I said, 'I'm not very happy at work.'" contains a statement in the Simple Present Tense ("I'm not very happy").

• Rule — Reported Speech (Statement, backshift of tense): when the reporting verb ("said") is in the past tense, the reported (present tense) verb inside the quotation shifts one step back — Simple Present → Simple Past. Also, "said to" changes to "told" when a listener is mentioned, and the pronoun "I" in the quote changes according to the subject of the reporting clause.

• Applying the rule: "said" → "told her"; "I'm not very happy" (Simple Present) → "I was not very happy" (Simple Past). This gives: "I told her that I was not very happy at work."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "I told her I would not be very happy at work." is incorrect because "would" wrongly converts the statement into a future-in-the-past/conditional sense, which is not present in the original statement.

• Option 3: "I told her that I had not been very happy at work." is incorrect because "had not been" is Past Perfect, which is used to backshift the Present Perfect Tense, not the Simple Present Tense used in the original quote.

• Option 4: "I told her I am not very happy at work." is incorrect because it fails to backshift the tense at all — "am" should change to "was" when reported using the past tense reporting verb "told".

NOTE

• General tense-backshift rule in narration: Simple Present → Simple Past; Present Continuous → Past Continuous; Present Perfect → Past Perfect; Simple Past → Past Perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might.

• "Say to" changes to "tell" in indirect speech only when the person addressed is mentioned (e.g., "said to me" → "told me"); otherwise "say" remains "say" (→ "said" stays "said").

question:
Fill in the blank with the most suitable word.
The scientists ______ that the chefs relied on a specific motion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. found.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "found" (past tense of "find") is used here in the sense of "discovered" or "concluded after investigation/research" — a standard usage in describing the outcome of a scientific study.
◦ Example: The researchers found that regular exercise improves memory.

• The sentence describes scientists reporting a research conclusion about chefs' technique ("relied on a specific motion"), and "found that..." is the natural collocation used to introduce such a research finding.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "invented" means to create something new that did not exist before — scientists cannot "invent" a fact about what chefs do; this does not fit the context of a finding/observation.

• Option 2: "innovated" means to introduce new methods or ideas — it does not fit the context of reporting an observed fact.

• Option 3: "planned" means to decide on and arrange something in advance — it does not fit the context of describing a research conclusion.

NOTE

• Common verbs used to report research findings: found, discovered, observed, concluded, revealed, established.

• Distinguish carefully: invent (create something new), discover/find (become aware of something that already existed), innovate (introduce new methods).

question:
Select the word segment that substitutes (replaces) the bracketed word segment correctly and completes the sentence meaningfully. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.
Nonetheless, (many an old poets, such as Tennyson and Browning, has) kept their romances to the end.
option_1: many old poets, such as Tennyson and Browning, have
option_2: many old poets, such Tennyson and Browning, has
option_4: many a old poets, such Tennyson and Browning, has
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. many old poets, such as Tennyson and Browning, have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "many an old poet" uses the singular construction "many a + singular noun", which must take a singular verb (e.g., "many a poet has"). However, the original sentence uses the plural noun "poets" together with "many an", which is grammatically inconsistent.

• Rule: "Many a" is always followed by a singular noun + singular verb (e.g., "Many a student has failed"), while "Many" (without "a") is followed by a plural noun + plural verb (e.g., "Many students have failed"). Since the sentence lists two specific poets ("Tennyson and Browning") — inherently plural in sense — the correct form is "many old poets... have".

• Applying the rule: "many an old poets...has" is corrected to "many old poets, such as Tennyson and Browning, have", restoring agreement between the plural subject and the plural verb "have".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "many old poets, such Tennyson and Browning, has" is incorrect because it drops the necessary word "as" after "such" (it should be "such as"), and it also wrongly retains the singular verb "has" with the plural subject "poets".

• Option 3: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original bracketed phrase clearly contains a grammatical error (mixing "many an" with a plural noun and verb), so improvement is required.

• Option 4: "many a old poets, such Tennyson and Browning, has" is incorrect because "many a" must be followed by "an" (not "a") before a vowel sound and, more importantly, by a singular noun ("poet"), not the plural "poets"; it also drops "as" after "such" and keeps the singular verb "has" wrongly.

NOTE

• Fixed structures to remember: "Many a + singular noun + singular verb" (e.g., Many a man has died); "Many + plural noun + plural verb" (e.g., Many men have died).

• "Such as" (not just "such") is the correct phrase used to introduce examples (e.g., "poets, such as Tennyson and Browning").

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
We are the creative force of our life, and through our own decisions rather than our conditions, if we carefully learn to do certain things, we can ______ those goals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. accomplish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "accomplish" means to achieve or successfully complete something, such as a task or a goal. It is the standard collocation used with the noun "goals" in English.
◦ Example: With careful planning, the team was able to accomplish all its goals for the year.

• The sentence talks positively about using one's own decisions to reach one's "goals", and "accomplish those goals" is the only option that logically and grammatically fits this positive sense of achievement.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "expel" means to force someone to leave a place or organisation — it does not collocate with "goals" and contradicts the positive tone of the sentence.

• Option 3: "torment" means to cause severe suffering to someone — it does not fit the context of achieving personal goals.

• Option 4: "reverberate" means to be repeated as an echoing sound, or to continue to have effects — it does not logically combine with "goals" in this sentence.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "goals": achieve goals, accomplish goals, attain goals, reach goals, set goals, pursue goals.

• Distinguish: accomplish (successfully complete a task/goal) vs. accompany (go along with someone) — these are sometimes confused due to similar spelling.

Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, born on February 5th, 1985 and commonly known 1.__________ Cristiano Ronaldo, is a Portuguese footballer who 2.__________ as a forward for Spanish club Real Madrid and serves as captain 3.____________ the Portuguese national team. Ronaldo currently holds the distinction of being the most expensive player in football history after 4.____________ transferred to Real Madrid from Manchester United in a deal worth £80 million (€94m, US$132m). His contract with Real Madrid is believed to have made him the highest-paid 5.__________ player in the world.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that connects the verb "known" with the name that follows it — the fixed phrase is "known as", used to state the name or title by which someone/something is called.
◦ Example: He is commonly known as the "King of Pop".

• Applying this to the passage: "...commonly known as Cristiano Ronaldo..." correctly introduces the name he is popularly called by.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "at" is a preposition of place/time/point and does not collocate with "known" to introduce a name.

• Option 2: "for" would suggest "known for" (a reason/quality he is famous for), which does not fit before a proper name introduced immediately after "commonly known".

• Option 3: "in" is a preposition of place/time and does not collocate with "known" in this naming sense.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositional phrases with "known": known as (called by a name), known for (famous for a quality/reason), known to (familiar to someone).

• Similar structures: referred to as, called, termed, dubbed.

question:

Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, born on February 5th, 1985 and commonly known 1.__________ Cristiano Ronaldo, is a Portuguese footballer who 2.__________ as a forward for Spanish club Real Madrid and serves as captain 3.____________ the Portuguese national team. Ronaldo currently holds the distinction of being the most expensive player in football history after 4.____________ transferred to Real Madrid from Manchester United in a deal worth £80 million (€94m, US$132m). His contract with Real Madrid is believed to have made him the highest-paid 5.__________ player in the world.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. plays.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage describes Cristiano Ronaldo using the Simple Present Tense throughout ("is a Portuguese footballer", "serves as captain") to state general, ongoing facts about him.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense (third person singular): Subject (he/she/it) + V1 + s/es. Since the subject "who" here refers back to "Cristiano Ronaldo" (a singular, third-person subject), the verb must take the "-s" form.

• Applying the rule: "...a Portuguese footballer who plays as a forward for Spanish club Real Madrid..." correctly uses the present-tense, third-person-singular form to match the surrounding tense of the passage.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "played" is Simple Past Tense, which breaks the Simple Present Tense used consistently throughout the rest of the passage.

• Option 3: "will play" is Simple Future Tense, which does not match the passage's description of Ronaldo's ongoing, present role.

• Option 4: "has played" is Present Perfect Tense, which suggests a completed action with present relevance rather than an ongoing, habitual role as described elsewhere in the passage.

NOTE

• In cloze passages, always check the surrounding verbs to identify the tense used consistently in the passage before selecting the blank's tense.

• Third-person singular present tense verbs always add -s/-es (he plays, she watches, it goes) unless a modal (can, will, may) precedes them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a preposition that correctly links the noun "captain" with the group or team being captained — the fixed phrase is "captain of" (a team/country/side).
◦ Example: She serves as the captain of the national hockey team.

• Applying this to the passage: "...serves as captain of the Portuguese national team" correctly identifies which team Ronaldo captains.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "in" does not collocate with "captain" in the sense of leading a specific team; "captain in" is not idiomatic English.

• Option 2: "with" does not fit the meaning of holding the position of leader of a specific team.

• Option 4: "at" is a preposition of place/time and does not collocate with "captain" to show which team is led.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositional phrase: "captain of" a team/side/country (e.g., captain of India, captain of the ship).

• Similarly fixed: "member of", "president of", "head of" — all use "of" to link a role/title to the group it belongs to.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Fill in the blanks with the help of the alternatives given. Select the most appropriate option for each blank.

Cristiano Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, born on February 5th, 1985 and commonly known 1.__________ Cristiano Ronaldo, is a Portuguese footballer who 2.__________ as a forward for Spanish club Real Madrid and serves as captain 3.____________ the Portuguese national team. Ronaldo currently holds the distinction of being the most expensive player in football history after 4.____________ transferred to Real Madrid from Manchester United in a deal worth £80 million (€94m, US$132m). His contract with Real Madrid is believed to have made him the highest-paid 5.__________ player in the world.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No.4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. having.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank follows the preposition "after", which must be followed by a gerund (verb + -ing) form when introducing an action that happened before the main action described in the sentence.

• Rule: prepositions (such as "after", "before", "on", "since") are always followed by a gerund, never a base form or infinitive, when introducing a clause describing an action. The perfect gerund "having + V3" (here, "having transferred") is used to emphasise that the transfer was completed before Ronaldo attained "the most expensive player" distinction.

• Applying the rule: "...holds the distinction... after having transferred to Real Madrid from Manchester United in a deal worth £80 million..." correctly uses the perfect gerund after the preposition "after".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "been" cannot directly follow "after" on its own without an auxiliary such as "having" (e.g., "after having been") — "after been transferred" is not grammatically complete.

• Option 2: "is" is a finite present-tense verb form and cannot follow a preposition like "after", which requires a gerund, not a finite verb.

• Option 4: "be" is a base/infinitive form and, like "is", cannot directly follow the preposition "after"; only a gerund form is grammatically permissible here.

NOTE

• Rule to remember: preposition + gerund (verb-ing), never preposition + base verb or finite verb — e.g., "before leaving", "on arriving", "since joining".

• The perfect gerund "having + V3" is used to stress that one action was completed before another action or state, both in active ("having finished his work, he left") and passive ("having been transferred") senses.
